paras: The lynching of Tom Williams was the burning of a Black man by a crowd on the courthouse square at Sulphur Springs, Hopkins County, Texas, on August 11, 1905. Accused of attempting to assault a young white girl, he was taken from officers and burned after she identified him. The burning drew Black-press editorials and a later dispute over a Texas Negro Baptist convention's reported endorsement of it.

Williams, described as a "mulatto," was about 30 by one report and about 35 by another, which said he had done odd jobs in town for two years. The girl lived on a farm about two miles from town; most reports named her Nettie Griggs, but the Baltimore Afro-American and Richmond Planet called her Mary Childs.

According to the Ardmoreite's special report, at about six o'clock a man sprang from the bushes, held a knife to her throat, and fled when she screamed. The Palestine Daily Herald said he beat her and tore her clothes, and The Sun that he choked her unconscious.

After a search, officers caught Williams, by The Sun's account hiding in a barn two miles from the scene. At the square a mob of "fully 2000 men" took him from them, according to the Palestine paper; the wire report said "little resistance was made to the mob by the officers." He was shot in an arm, the bullet slightly wounding a white man, or through the hand.

Brought before the girl, he was identified, and she is reported to have exclaimed "Burn him!" or "Take him away and burn him." The Sun and a dispatch summarized by the Washington Bee said he then confessed. His clothing was soaked in coal oil, and he was chained to a stake or, by two accounts, strung from a tree limb. The body was later cut down and burned again, and his relatives took the remains.
Estimates of the crowd ranged from "several hundred" to about 3,000. A Dallas dispatch said the leaders were prominent life-long citizens who made no attempt to disguise themselves.

The Sun reported that the coroner took the body down and returned a verdict of "Death by mob violence." A Dallas dispatch said the governor would investigate; no report of an investigation, arrest or trial appears in the coverage.

The Sun described "general satisfaction" in the town and threats against "worthless negroes" that caused a "hurried exodus of many." On August 14 Jim Cherry, a Black man who had spoken against the girl's character, was beaten and ordered out of town. Black Baptist groups moved their state conventions from the town to Dallas, saying it "was not a safe place for negroes."

Dispatches later reported that the Negro Baptist state convention, meeting in Dallas on August 25, had commended the burning; an Ohio Methodist Episcopal district conference condemned that stand the next day. The Oklahoma Safeguard, quoting the Portland Advocate, called those who endorsed it accessories, while the Liberator doubted the endorsement.

White papers carried a Dallas dispatch and a short wire item on August 11, the Daily Tribune headlining that the "Terrible Sight Sickens Spectators." The Ardmoreite described "Frenzied Citizens" capturing a "Fiend," and The Sun headlined "Negro Burns for His Crime" and wrote that "The terrible punishment was given for a terrible crime."

Black weeklies reprinted the wire item and a narrative headed "Hundreds of People Stand Around And Enjoy The Fun." Their editorials condemned rape and the burning alike: the Muskogee Cimeter wrote "No mob law in ours," and the Richmond Planet noted "no allegation that he accomplished his purpose." The Baltimore Afro-American asked why no one in authority had spoken, and the Washington Bee called the burning "more brutal than the alleged offense." The Topeka Plaindealer charged that the district judge and county officials had taken part, a claim the Atlanta Independent reprinted as "incendiary language."

Accounts differ on the girl's name, her age (14 or 17), the hour of the attack, and the manner of burning. The reports closest to the scene, from Sulphur Springs and other Texas towns, consistently name her Nettie Griggs.

reader.title: Lynching of Tom Williams
bases: A crowd took Williams, accused of attacking a white girl, from officers and burned him on the public square at Sulphur Springs (A3, A7, A9).

Williams was burned to death by a mob put at 2,000 to 3,000 people without trial (A3, A9, A13); the papers present it as punishment for an alleged assault on a white girl, and the coroner's verdict was 'Death by mob violence' (A7).
Independent local and wire reports from Sulphur Springs, Dallas and Palestine agree on the burning, the place and the accusation (A2, A3, A4, A9, A30).

accounts.label: Sulphur Springs special (Ardmoreite)
accounts.gist: Williams, about 30, seized Nettie Griggs at knifepoint at 6 a.m., fled, was caught four miles away, identified, chained to a stake and burned at 9:30 by about 3,000 'best citizens'.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: A negro charged with assaulting a widow's daughter was pursued, captured, chained to a stake in the court house square and burned; officers made little resistance.

accounts.label: The Sun's account
accounts.gist: Officers caught Williams in a barn at dawn and were forced to give him up; he confessed after identification; the coroner found 'Death by mob violence'; threats drove many Black residents away.

accounts.label: Palestine Daily Herald (Texas dispatch)
accounts.gist: A mob of 2,000 took Williams from officers at the square; he was shot in an arm, the bullet wounding a white man; burned between 10 and 11 a.m.

accounts.label: Dallas dispatch / later wire
accounts.gist: Williams was strung from a tree limb, oiled and burned, cut down and burned again; prominent citizens led the mob undisguised.

accounts.label: Account printed in Black weeklies
accounts.gist: Williams, 'a mulatto Negro', accosted Mary Childs in a pasture; caught by officers and a posse, identified, oiled and burned; relatives took the remains.

accounts.label: Topeka Plaindealer
accounts.gist: Alleged that the district judge and county officials participated, citing an Associated Press clipping.

framing.detail: Ardmoreite: 'Frenzied Citizens Capture Fiend', burned by 'our best citizens'; Palestine Herald: 'His Atrocious Act', 'miscreant'.
The Sun: 'Negro Burns for His Crime'; 'The terrible punishment was given for a terrible crime'; 'general satisfaction'.
Short neutral wire item ('In Court House Yard', 'Negro Burned at Stake').
Daily Tribune: 'Terrible Sight Sickens Spectators'; Omaha Bee and Hawaiian Star note 'another negro' burned in Texas, the Star citing race prejudice.
Editorials in the Cimeter, Planet, Afro-American, Bee, Plaindealer and Liberator condemned the burning while condemning rape.
The Atlanta Independent called the Plaindealer's charge against officials 'incendiary language'.
Freeman and Oklahoma Safeguard condemned the Texas Negro Baptist convention's reported endorsement.
